elements.text: I would discourage the integration of any PRNG algorithm into the code for three reasons. (1) libbitcoin passes this call to the operating system (through boost I believe). This allows integration with hardware random number generation. (2) Software cannot produce random numbers, so we discourage the use of even our own single API for this in any security context relating to bitcoin. Even bx allows all seeds to be input as arguments. We do not want to imply otherwise. (3) It is more code to maintain, and non-trivial.

text: I would discourage the integration of any PRNG algorithm into the code for three reasons. (1) libbitcoin passes this call to the operating system (through boost I believe). This allows integration with hardware random number generation. (2) Software cannot produce random numbers, so we discourage the use of even our own single API for this in any security context relating to bitcoin. Even bx allows all seeds to be input as arguments. We do not want to imply otherwise. (3) It is more code to maintain, and non-trivial.

elements.text: I generally agree, but I'm not sure PRNG has the option for hardware random number generation, since at least on systems like GNU/Linux, it sources from a pseudo-random pool (/dev/urandom).
libsodium

claims it has the hardware true random capability if it's available.  Either way, I think point 3 is the most important in some sense, as if we provide something that people believe is true random when in fact, that can't be provided in a general configuration, it's a maintenance/support/security burden taken on for no concrete benefit.

Either way, I think point 3 is the most important in some sense, as if we provide something that people believe is true random when in fact, that can't be provided in a general configuration, it's a maintenance/support/security burden taken on for no concrete benefit.

attachments.text:
The Mersenne Twister is a pseudorandom number generator (PRNG). It is by far the most widely used general-purpose PRNG. Its name derives from the fact that its period length is chosen to be a Mersenne prime.
The Mersenne Twister was developed in 1997 by Makoto Matsumoto (松本 眞) and Takuji Nishimura (西村 拓士). It was designed specifically to rectify most of the flaws found in older PRNGs.
The most commonly used version of the Mersenne Twister algorithm is based on the Mersenne prime 219937−1.  The standard implementation of that, MT19937, uses a 32-bit word length. There is another implementation (with five variants) that uses a 64-bit word length, MT19937-64; it generates a different sequence.

text: `/dev/random` uses OS level entropy (sourced from hardware events).  `/dev/urandom` is pseudo-random that is less random than `/dev/random`, but it provides quicker access to pseudo-random values.  If you try to read data from `/dev/urandom`, you can read large quantities.  If you try to read data from `/dev/random`, you will find that you are often blocking, waiting for the system to provide more entropy

attachments.text: In Unix-like operating systems, /dev/random, /dev/urandom and /dev/arandom are special files that serve as pseudorandom number generators. They allow access to environmental noise collected from device drivers and other sources.   /dev/random typically blocks if there is less entropy available than requested; /dev/urandom typically never blocks, even if the pseudorandom number generator seed was not fully initialized with entropy since boot. /dev/arandom blocks after boot until the seed has been securely initialized with enough entropy, and then never blocks again. Not all operating systems implement the same methods for /dev/random and /dev/urandom and only a few provide /dev/arandom.

elements.text:
"/dev/random versus /dev/urandom
And now we get to the meat of the issue- which output interface to use for "the most demanding cryptographic computational long-term security"? First thing is first- both /dev/random and /dev/urandom are fed data from the same CSPRNG. Let me repeat that, with a bit more emphasis: Both /dev/random and /dev/urandom are fed data from the same CSPRNG. In fact, most who understand this, will explain that you should use /dev/urandom, and NOT /dev/random. The problem is, that /dev/random has the horrible bug of blocking when the input entropy pool is exhausted. So, if your application relies on /dev/random to get random numbers, there are pauses and delays until there is enough entropy in the input pool to reseed the CSPRNG, so you can get more data."

elements.text: No problem.  Regardless of which entropy source is a user's preferred method, libbitcoin's stance has generally been to never use system generated random values for anything related to storing coins, which is why the model chosen is to allow a user to provide their own entropy.  If someone believes /dev/urandom is "good enough", they can pass in generated values on the command line.  Others may believe that dice rolls are "good enough", so those can be passed in too.  In other words, regardless of what I think about the GNU/Linux sources of randomness, libbitcoin doesn't necessarily prefer either where it matters.

elements.text:
From what I understand, the Liquid sidechain is a permissioned network where node operators essentially sign blocks. A block is considered final once 2/3rd of the nodes have signed a block. It is a pretty straight forward majority based consensus algorithm, with no byzantine fault tolerance because you trust the nodes.

And since you trust nodes (which I think will largely be exchanges and financial institutions) they will be pretty obedient of the state, unless of course they chose to do whatever they do, fuck things up and then ask for a bail out. But I digress.

I think Liquid and other sidechains (if any follow) will make bitcoin more accessible to financial institutions, so in all this is great stuff, if you want that. But once you peg your bitcoin off the bitcoin blockchain into a sidechain, you are completely in state/fintech land.
